title: Where does your electricity actually come from?
subtitle: An invisible mix
subject: comprendreLeMonde
description: At the socket, nothing says whether the power came from the sun, the wind or a coal plant. Behind that everyday gesture lies a mix that changes by the hour, and sometimes crosses borders.
author: rana-abdalla

hero.hook: The plug is the same everywhere. What lies behind it never is.

blocks.text: You plug in your phone, and electricity arrives without a label. Nothing at the socket says whether it was made from sunlight, water behind a dam or fuel burned at a power plant. Even two homes on the same street cannot point to the plant that each unit of their power comes from.

The reason is simple: almost every home draws on an [[electricity grid]], a network of wires linking power plants and users across an area. Several plants feed it at the same time, and their respective shares make up the [[electricity mix]]. That mix describes the sources supplying the network, not a separate stream of solar or gas electricity sent straight to your phone. The answer therefore begins well beyond the walls of your home.

Coal plants and many nuclear plants use heat to make steam. That steam spins a [[turbine]], a set of blades connected to a [[generator]], the machine that turns movement into electricity. Gas plants can also spin their turbines directly with the hot gases from combustion. Different processes, but the same electricity, flowing into the same grid.

blocks.caption: The turbine hall of a power plant: the steam turbine is coupled to its generator.

blocks.text: Wind turbines turn with the wind, hydropower plants with flowing water. Solar panels take a different route: they produce electricity directly from light, with no spinning blades at all. These sources do not work under the same conditions. Solar output falls when the sun sets, and wind generation changes with the weather. Plants that burn fuel can then supply power when the others produce less.
A nuclear plant works, at heart, like a coal plant: heat boils water, and it is the steam that drives the turbine. Only the source of heat changes.

sections.title: A mix that changes through the day

blocks.text: At noon, solar panels are working flat out while offices and homes draw power. After sunset they stop, but lamps, trains and kitchens still need electricity. A windy afternoon can also give way to a calm evening, while consumption rises or falls.

blocks.caption: The control room of a grid operator: the wall of screens shows the state of the network in real time.

blocks.text: The [[grid operator]], the organization that runs this network, must keep supply and demand in balance at all times. Some power stations adjust their output. Where batteries are installed, they release electricity stored earlier. Other sources fill the gap left by the fading sun. There is no daily recipe: the mix at noon can look very different from the mix a few hours later, even though your socket has not changed.

In 2025, about **a quarter** (24%) of the electricity generated at large power plants in the United States came from [[renewable sources]], the ones nature replenishes on its own: sunlight, wind, flowing water. That figure, still preliminary, describes the whole year. It does not mean renewables supplied the same share every time someone switched on a kettle or charged a phone.

A yearly percentage blends sunny afternoons, windy nights and the periods when sun and wind produce little. It also adds up hours of high and low demand. To know which sources are supplying a grid at a given moment, you need its hour-by-hour mix rather than its yearly average. Both views are useful, but they do not answer the same question.

The hourly mix still needs one more detail: which electricity is actually available in your area. A power station on one side of a border can feed the grid on the other side. That imported electricity blends with local generation. The [[consumption mix]], meaning the sources supplying the users of an area, can therefore differ from the mix produced on the spot.

blocks.caption: The Bełchatów coal plant in Poland, the largest in Europe.

blocks.text: This matters for the emissions linked to your electricity. Burning coal or gas releases carbon dioxide, a gas that warms the planet. Wind turbines, solar panels and nuclear plants do not release it directly while producing power. Electricity does not stop at the border, and neither does its impact. Depending on where the imports come from, the emissions tied to your consumption can be higher or lower than local generation alone suggests.
The electricity at your socket is a mix that changes by the hour and crosses borders, so neither the yearly average nor local generation alone tells you where it comes from.
